LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST CONCEPTS · AGES 18–24 MONTHS

Down — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson lands the pair: after up comes down, taught with a crouch, a drop, and a voice that slides downward. Show the two cards back to back and the contrast does the teaching.

What is this?

Down is a direction word — the way the ball goes, the way you crouch, the way everything dropped ends up. The card shows an object positioned down, and the floor is its natural address.

What does it mean?

Down is physical comedy for toddlers: things that go down usually land with a satisfying noise. The word rides the drop, and the crouch puts your toddler’s own body into the lesson.

What does the child need to know?

Expect a crouch, a drop performed on cue, or dow! said at the landing — all are answers. The word arrives mid-action best: say down as the ball falls, not after it stops.

Why this matters

Down is the most demonstrated direction in the house — cups off tables, blocks off trays, toddlers down slides. A word this well-illustrated by physics needs only naming.

What it teaches

Direction vocabulary on the second pole, cause-and-effect delight, and the body knowledge of high and low — spatial grammar with sound effects.

Words to learn

downlowdropfloorcrouchfall

Say this to your child

“"Down! Crouch down low, low, low… can you touch the floor? Watch the ball — up high… down! It fell down! Say down! Again? Ready… down!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the up card for one beat — up! — then the down card, and slide your voice and your crouch downward: dooown.
  2. Invite the crouch: can you go down low? A toddler folded down to the floor is the word wearing a body.
  3. Drop the ball: hold a soft ball high, say ready… and release on down! The word timed to the fall is the whole lesson in one second.
  4. Let your toddler run the drop: their hand, their timing, your voice on cue. Dropping and naming beats any worksheet ever printed.
  5. Pair them all week: stretch up, fold down; ball up, ball down. The switch is where the concept sharpens — and the giggles are where it stays.

Look closer at the picture

The card shows an object positioned down for toddler concept learning — one thing placed low. Ask your toddler to point at it, then to crouch all the way down until their fingers touch the floor.

Ask your child

"Can you crouch down low?" "Where did the ball go?" "Which way is down?" "What goes down after up?"

What your child can say or do

A crouch, a ball delivered over the edge of the tray with eye contact, or dow! at the thud — all are the lesson landing. Expect repeat requests for the drop; the physics is doing half the teaching.

Out in the real world

Down demonstrates itself constantly: the cup pushed off the table, the slide, the stairs, the sun going down. Name the falls gently and the daily crashes become vocabulary.

Try it together

Ready-set-drop: stand at the sofa arm with three soft balls, count ready… and drop on down! — then let your toddler call the word while you drop. Caller and dropper swap after three; both jobs teach.

Understanding check

Show both cards and ask for down. A crouch, a point at the low card, or a demonstrated drop all pass. Then drop something on purpose in the kitchen — a named down at the thud means the word has left the cards.

Parent tips

Say the word as the thing falls — timing is what welds word to event. Keep the pair moving: up-down games beat single-word drills at this age, and the switch is where the thinking happens.

Staying safe

The dropping game uses soft balls and safe heights — sofa arms and rug landings only, nothing that bounces toward faces. Crouching toddlers have low centres of gravity but zero judgement: clear the coffee table edges first.

This lesson pairs with the Down flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Concepts (Toddler 2).
